Both of these concepts work mechanically, but the paddle-wheel (spin plate) approach is significantly more reliable and forgiving than the dual-flywheel (Nerf-style) setup for dry extruded pellets.

Why Dual Flywheels Struggle with Food Pellets

While Nerf flywheels work brilliantly on flexible, uniform EVA foam darts, extruded cereal and fish pellets (like AquaMax or Game Fish Chow) introduce distinct physical failure points:

  • Brittleness vs. Crushing: Even with squishy silicone or TPU rollers, extruded pellets have zero tensile elasticity. Once compressed enough to overcome static friction, they tend to shatter into meal and dust rather than spring forward.
  • Dust Build-up & Slip: The high-friction surface required to throw the pellet quickly glazes over with fish oil and starch dust, causing the wheels to slip and stall.
  • Feed Jamming: If three pellets drop into the wheel gap simultaneously, rigid interference will instantly bind the motors or strip drive gears.

The Standard Commercial Blueprint (And How to Build It)

Most commercial pond feeders (like Texas Hunter or Moultrie) use a two-stage separation of metering and throwing to handle 7–8 handfuls (~1.5–2 cups) cleanly without turning the food into powder.

       [ Conical Hopper ]
               │
      [ Slow Metering Stage ]  ──> (Auger / Rotary Valve / Solenoid Slide Gate)
               │
    [ High-Speed Spinner Plate ] ──> (Throws 15-25 ft into pond)
  1. Metering Stage (Controls Quantity): A slow-moving component drops the exact volume needed into the thrower.
    • Best DIY option: A small 12V 30–60 RPM slow-gear auger or a rotary paddle valve. Running it for 3–5 seconds drops the exact 7–8 handfuls you need.
  2. Throwing Stage (Provides Velocity):
    • A high-speed DC motor (12V, 2,000–4,000 RPM) spins a flat disc with 2–4 upright paddles angled slightly backward (to cup and launch rather than crush).
    • Tilting the plate at a 15° to 30° upward angle gives you the optimal ballistic trajectory to throw buoyant pellets 15 to 25 feet across the water surface.

Outdoor Reliability Considerations

  • Moisture & Condensation: Floating fish pellets are hygroscopic. Water evaporation off the pond will rise into the discharge chute, making pellets sticky within 48 hours. A mechanical spring-loaded drop gate that stays closed until the spinner activates prevents humidity from traveling up the chute.
  • Critter Defense: Raccoons and squirrels will shake the feeder to drop food. A recessed spin plate or an enclosed deflector shield keeps paws from reaching the drop tube.

  2. Dispense (Run-Time Tuned): Gate opens or auger runs to drop the 7–8 handfuls directly into the center of the spinning plate.

  4. Shutdown & Seal: Spinner coasts down; physical seal confirms closure.

Sealing & Metering: Two Mechanical Approaches

A linear pull-type 12V solenoid works for a shutter gate, but solenoids present a common failure mode with granular feeds: pellet bridging / shearing. If a pellet is halfway through the aperture when the solenoid de-energizes, the return spring often lacks the shear strength to cut through the pellet, leaving the gate stuck partially cracked (inviting humidity and bugs).

  • Weighted Rubber Flapper: A silicone rubber one-way flapper door at the bottom of the drop chute. The weight of falling pellets pushed by a low-RPM auger effortlessly nudges it open, but ambient pond humidity and insects cannot push past the sealed resting flap.

If you pair an auger with an active door mechanism, there are a few ways to make the seal jam-proof while keeping precise electronic control.

Why the Foam Seal Concept Works (and Where It Fails)

  • The Advantage: A thick foam or silicone plug can deform around a trapped pellet, maintaining an airtight/moisture seal on both sides without stalling the actuator.
  • The Failure Mode: If the door slides across an opening with a stray pellet, the shear force will tear open-cell foam or bind the track. The motion needs to be a direct compression clamp or a compliant wiper.

Jam-Resilient Electronic Door Designs

1. The Silicone Iris / Pinch Valve (Highest Reliability)

  • Instead of a rigid slide door, run a short section of flexible, food-safe silicone tubing at the auger exit.
  • A high-torque metal-gear servo or linear actuator presses a rounded anvil against the silicone tube to pinch it shut.
  • If pellets are caught inside when pinched, the silicone tube simply bulges around them while sealing the surrounding gap, with zero shear stress on the motor.

2. Compliant Rotary Flap (Servo-Driven)

  • A 180° metal-gear servo drives a thick silicone or EVA foam paddle over the chute opening.
  • Rather than a flat blade, use a soft silicone sweep blade (like a heavy-duty squeegee). If it encounters a pellet on closure, it flexes over the pellet and maintains contact with the rim.
  • Control trick: Program the servo to sweep back and forth 20° twice before seating to flick away stray pellets.

3. The Retracting Auger (Zero Extra Actuators)

  • You can combine the door and the auger into a single active assembly using a push-pull mechanism:
    • Mount the auger on a splined shaft or keyed slider.
    • A spring keeps a conical soft-rubber plug at the tip of the auger pressed firmly against the discharge nozzle.
    • When the auger motor energizes, a small linear solenoid or cam pulls the auger back 1/2 inch to unseat the cone, allowing pellets to flow through the flighting.

Control Sequence with Active Feedback

If you run a servo or motor-driven door, you can add stall/current detection to make it completely fail-safe:

  1. Open Door: Actuator clears chute $\rightarrow$ Verify limit switch / position.
  2. Spin-Up: Throwing plate reaches target RPM.
  3. Auger Run: Dispense 7–8 handfuls based on rotation count or runtime.
  4. Auger Reverse Pulse: Run the auger in reverse for 200 ms to retract trailing pellets back into the tube.
  5. Close Door: Move actuator to seal position. If a stall is detected (pellet trapped), back off 10 mm, pulse the thrower, and re-clamp.

Key Design Specs for Large-Bore Pinch Valves

  • Tubing Spec:
    • Inner Diameter (ID): 1.5" to 2.0" (keeps pellets flowing freely with zero wall drag).
    • Wall Thickness: 1.5 mm to 2.0 mm (thin enough to fold flat without excessive motor torque, thick enough to resist tearing).
    • Material: Platinum-cured translucent silicone hose (stays pliable down into freezing temperatures and won't harden under outdoor UV).
  • Pinch Bar Geometry:
    • Use a rounded cylindrical bar (radius $\ge$ 6–8 mm) rather than a flat or wedge profile.
    • A rounded bar rolls and compresses the silicone evenly without creating high shear stress along the fold creases.
  • Actuation Mechanism:
    • Cam / Crank Linkage: A standard metal-gear standard servo (like an MG996R or DS3218 with 15–20 kg·cm torque) driving a simple offset arm gives you mechanical advantage at the close point, delivering peak clamping force right as the tubing collapses.
    • Over-Center Lock: Setting the servo linkage so it sits slightly past top-dead-center when closed means the valve stays locked shut mechanically without continuous motor stall current.

Print & Assembly Considerations

  • Slit-Free Housing: Design the enclosing body with a drain/weep channel beneath the tube clamp so any stray moisture or pellet dust falls straight through to the spinner rather than settling inside the pivot bearings.
  • Tubing Retention: Secure the top and bottom of the silicone sleeve over barbed rigid collars with zip ties or hose clamps to keep the tube from creeping downward during repeated clamp cycles.

The pre-batched approach trades mechanical metering complexity for indexing/packaging design. The real trick here is avoiding the need to mechanically unpack or manipulate soft/flexible packaging like Ziploc bags, which jam easily and leave plastic waste in the mechanism.

Instead, the containers themselves should serve as rigid, reusable mechanical buckets that either tip, drop a false bottom, or ride a simple carousel/magazine.

Three Core Batch-Feed Architectures

1. The Revolving Carousel / "Lazy Susan" (Lowest Mechanical Complexity)

  • Mechanism: A circular disc with 7–14 individual cylindrical pockets (or standard 8–16 oz deli cups without lids) arranged in a ring. A top stationary cover seals all chambers from rain except for a single drop hole positioned directly above your spinner thrower.
  • Operation: A stepper or geared motor advances the plate by one position per feeding. The cup moves over the drop port, the pellets fall straight through into the high-speed spinner, and the spinner flings them into the pond.
  • Why it works: The food drops purely by gravity; no opening lids or tearing bags required.

2. Gravity-Fed Magazine Tube (Vertical Stack / Pez Dispenser)

  • Mechanism: Rigid, stackable round pucks/cups with hinged swing bottoms or open-top cups stacked vertically inside a PVC or 3D-printed tube.
  • Operation: A single linear actuator or solenoid kicks the bottom cup forward:
    • As the cup slides over a drop chute, a bottom trapdoor swings down (or drops through a slot), dumping the 7–8 handfuls into the spinner.
    • The empty cup drops into a collection bin or remains in a secondary stack.

3. Revolving Drum / Gatling Hopper (Compact Multi-Day Storage)

  • Mechanism: A horizontal or tilted cylinder divided into 6–8 pie-shaped wedge chambers.
  • Operation: A small ratchet mechanism or servo indexes the barrel 45°–60° per cycle. As a chamber reaches the 6 o'clock position, its contents drop out of the slot directly into the throwing plate.

The spiral/corkscrew partition idea is conceptually very cool—it effectively turns a 1D vertical drop into a long, sequenced multi-day pipeline.

However, running a segmented helix introduces distinct geometric and mechanical realities that dictate how you load, drive, and dispense the food.

Mechanics of the Segmented Corkscrew

When you add dividing walls every 30° along a helical screw flight:

  1. Relative Motion & Drag:
    • In a standard open auger, the screw rotates inside a stationary outer cylinder to push bulk loose material along the trough.
    • If the screw has fixed radial bulkheads creating isolated cells, the entire helix and outer wall must either rotate together, or the bulkheads will scrape aggressively against a stationary outer wall, pinching pellets between the moving divider edges and the casing.
  2. The "Archimedes Bucket Elevator" Approach:
    • A more reliable execution is a segmented outer drum with internal spiral baffles.
    • As the drum indexes around a fixed central core, each pocket slides downward over a smooth interior track until it hits the final bottom index port.

Refilling Strategy: Segmented Stack vs. Cascade Filling

               │  [Level 1: Discharge ]  │

  • The Stacking Module (Cleanest): Design modular 3D-printed interlocking tiers (e.g., 3 to 4 rings stacked vertically). Each ring contains 6 to 8 wedge cavities. You load them from bottom to top, drop the next tier on, and key them together via a central hexagonal drive shaft.
  • The Cascade / Spillway Method: If you want a single-pour refill from the top, the radial dividers must have staggered weir notches. When Cell 1 fills to capacity, the excess spills over the baffle into Cell 2, and so forth down the spiral. The challenge here is ensuring equal volume per cell across varying pellet shapes.

Direct-Drop vs. Firing: Suspended Pond Mount

Suspending the entire unit over the pond on a taught high-line/cable eliminates the high-speed throwing motor entirely.

Passive "Shotgun" Dispersion:

  • Instead of an active motor spinning, place a 45° conical passive deflector 4–6 inches directly beneath the drop chute.
  • Pellets falling 3–6 feet from the suspended unit hit the rigid cone and scatter radially outward across a 6 to 10-foot circle on the water.
  • Adding a small 12V vibration puck or a serrated cone face further randomizes the ricochet angles, widening the spread without adding a fragile external motor.

Structural & Weather Factors for Cable Mounting

  • Pendulum Torque: When the internal indexing motor pulses to rotate the drum/helix, the suspended housing will want to twist in the opposite direction. Counteract this with a two-point bridle harness rather than a single suspension point.
  • Wind Drift & Water Vapor: Being suspended directly above the water table means 100% relative humidity on calm nights. A downward-flanged skirt around the drop port acts as a vapor barrier, preventing rising steam/humidity from condensing inside the lowest food cell.

Parametric Geometry Blueprint (OpenSCAD Reference)

// Parametric Modular Feeder Tier
$fn = 90;

outer_radius = 110;    // 220mm outer diameter
hub_radius = 15;        // 30mm central hub
tier_height = 60;       // Height per daily slice
wall_th = 2.4;          // Shell thickness
num_cells = 8;          // 8 feedings per tier
lip_h = 5.0;            // Weather-lap height
lip_clearance = 0.4;    // Radial clearance for nesting

module tier() {
    difference() {
        union() {
            // Main cylinder body
            cylinder(r = outer_radius, h = tier_height);
            // Top nesting male lip
            translate([0, 0, tier_height])
                cylinder(r = outer_radius - wall_th - lip_clearance, h = lip_h);
        }
        
        // Bottom nesting female socket
        translate([0, 0, -0.1])
            cylinder(r = outer_radius - wall_th, h = lip_h + 0.1);
        
        // Central hex shaft cutout (10mm hex)
        translate([0, 0, -1])
            cylinder(r = 6.0, h = tier_height + lip_h + 2, $fn = 6);
            
        // Hollow out feed pockets
        for (i = [0 : num_cells - 1]) {
            rotate([0, 0, i * (360 / num_cells)])
                pocket_cutout();
        }
    }
}

module pocket_cutout() {
    // Pie slice cutout logic leaving wall_th ribs
    rotate_extrude(angle = (360 / num_cells) - 3) {
        translate([hub_radius + wall_th, 0])
            square([outer_radius - hub_radius - (2 * wall_th), tier_height + lip_h + 1]);
    }
}

tier();

Print Settings for Outdoor Durability

  • Filament: PETG or ASA/ABS. Avoid standard PLA, as sun exposure and moisture will cause warping and bacterial growth on food-contact surfaces.
  • Perimeters: 4 to 6 walls with 30% gyroid infill for rigidity against torsional flex.
  • Seam Placement: Set seams to Random or Rear-Aligned to prevent a continuous zipper bead on the nesting lips that could cause sticking.

Assembly & Suspension Setup

  1. Stationary Baseplate: Fasten the baseplate to an aluminum bottom cross-brace. The 45° drop aperture sits directly over a 60° printed deflection cone suspended 4 inches below the base.
  2. Drive Mechanism: Mount a high-torque 12V 10–15 RPM worm-gear motor underneath the baseplate, driving the center hex shaft. The worm gearbox provides an automatic mechanical brake, preventing the drum from back-driving when weight is uneven.

turns.response_html:
This segmented hopper concept is incredibly robust because it relies on gravity and a single rotating axis. But moving from a CAD concept to an outdoor mechanism suspended over a pond introduces some specific physical challenges.

Let’s stress-test the design, find the likely failure points, and look at how to engineer around them.

Problem 1: The "Guillotine" Pinch

As the drum rotates, the rigid plastic walls of the pockets sweep over the stationary drop port. If a piece of cereal or a rigid pellet is halfway down the hole when the wall passes over, it gets trapped between two hard plastic edges. This will either stall the motor, shear the pellet into dust (gunking up the track), or crack the 3D print.

  • Evolution A (Mechanical): Design the bottom edge of the dividing walls with a 2mm slot, and insert a strip of flexible TPU filament or silicone rubber. The wall sweeps the food, but bends harmlessly if a pellet gets caught.
  • Evolution B (Geometrical): Design the drop port in the stationary base to be slightly larger than the cell above it, with a heavily chamfered (angled) trailing edge. Instead of acting like scissors, the edge encourages the pellet to roll downward into the void.

Problem 2: The Unbalanced Pendulum

If you empty Pocket 1, then Pocket 2, then Pocket 3, one side of the drum becomes completely empty while the other is full of heavy feed. Suspended from a cable, this shifting center of gravity will cause the entire feeder to tilt heavily to one side, which could cause internal binding on the central shaft.

  • The Software Fix (Star-Pattern Indexing): Instead of moving 45° to the adjacent pocket, you can solve a mechanical problem with code. If you drive this with an RP2040 or similar microcontroller, program the motor to rotate 135° (three pockets) per feeding.
  • The Sequence: It will empty pocket 1, then 4, then 7, then 2, then 5, then 8, then 3, then 6. The weight distribution remains perfectly balanced throughout the entire week without adding a single mechanical part.

Problem 3: The "Chimney Effect" (Moisture)

Suspended directly above a pond during humid summer months, the stationary drop port acts like a chimney. Evaporation rises straight up the hole and into whatever pocket is currently sitting above it, turning Cheerios or fish food into a sticky, moldy clump that will refuse to drop.

  • Evolution: The passive scatter cone suspended below the feeder can double as a moisture block. Alternatively, design a simple spring-loaded "trap door" on the drop port that only pushes open when the weight of the food drops on it, sealing the drum off from rising humidity the rest of the time.

Problem 4: Bridging and Arching

Cheerios and extruded pellets are notorious for "bridging"—locking together to form an arch over a hole instead of falling through.

  • Evolution: Avoid right angles inside the pockets. In your OpenSCAD script, you can apply a fillet or a steep slope (at least 60 degrees) to the inner hub and outer walls. Granular dynamics dictate that if the bottom opening is at least 3 to 4 times the diameter of the largest pellet, bridging is mathematically unlikely.

Problem 5: Refill Logistics

Taking it apart tier-by-tier on a swaying cable over the water is a recipe for dropping parts in the pond.

  • Evolution (The Cartridge System): The entire drum stack should slide off the central hex shaft as a single locked unit. You bring an empty cartridge inside, fill the pockets on a flat table, snap the weather cap on, and then carry the sealed unit out to the pond to simply drop onto the feeder's drive shaft.

The triangulated rigging is exactly how you solve the twist and tilt problem. By running an upper and lower line to each tree (a 4-point harness), you completely lock the feeder’s orientation in 3D space, counteracting any asymmetrical weight from the feed.

Pivoting to a zero-electronics, gravity-driven clockwork mechanism is a brilliant evolution. You are essentially building a grandfather clock weight-drive, but using the descent of the feeder itself as the energy source.

Here is how you can engineer the mechanics of a continuously lowering, self-timing batch feeder.

The Descent-Powered "Clockwork" Engine

To make the feeder's descent power the rotation, the support rope doesn't just tie to the top—it wraps around an internal central spool. As gravity pulls the feeder down, the rope unwinds, forcing the spool to rotate.

However, if you just hang it, it will freefall into the pond in two seconds. You need a way to drastically slow the descent, and a way to turn that slow, continuous motion into sudden "batches" of food.

1. Controlling the Speed (The Governor)

To stretch a 4-foot drop over an entire week, you need a high-ratio gear train connected to a governor.

  • The Air Brake (Music Box Style): The spool turns a large gear, which meshes with smaller and smaller pinions. The final, fastest-spinning gear is attached to a small fan (an air brake). Air resistance increases exponentially with speed, capping the feeder's descent at a very slow, predictable crawl (e.g., lowering 6 inches per day).
  • The Viscous Damper (Simpler DIY): Instead of complex gears, you attach the central spool directly to a heavy-duty rotary fluid damper (like those used to slowly lower heavy piano lids or industrial doors). The viscous silicone fluid inside limits rotation to a glacial pace.

2. Dribble vs. Batch: The "Snail Cam"

If the spool is directly connected to your food drum, it will turn continuously. The problem? Food will dribble out one Cheerio every 20 minutes. Fish respond best to a sudden "hatch" or handful of food; a slow dribble will just be eaten by birds or turtles, and single pellets won't have enough weight to push open your spring-loaded moisture cone.

To fix this, you decouple the spool from the drum using a Snail Cam and Trip-Spring (exactly how a mechanical clock stores energy to chime the hour):

  1. The spool rotates continuously, slowly turning a snail-shaped cam.
  2. As the cam turns, it pushes a lever, slowly winding a strong torsion spring connected to the food drum.
  3. When the cam reaches its cliff edge (say, every 8 hours), the lever slips off.
  4. SNAP: The torsion spring violently releases, indexing the food drum exactly 45 degrees in a fraction of a second.
  5. An entire pocket of food drops instantly.

3. The Kinetic Moisture Lock

This "snap" mechanism solves your moisture-lock problem beautifully.

Because an entire handful of food drops at high velocity all at once, it possesses enough kinetic energy to punch the bottom scatter-cone open against its spring. The food hits the cone, scatters outward, and the cone instantly snaps back up against the drop port, perfectly sealing the drum from rising pond humidity.

The Operating Cycle (A Week at the Pond)

  1. Sunday: You fill the drum cartridges. You walk out to the pond, push the feeder up the ropes to the top of its travel, and wind the internal spool.
  2. The Descent: For the next 7 days, gravity pulls the heavy feeder downward against the air brake/damper.
  3. The Feeding: Twice a day, the internal snail cam trips. The drum snaps 45 degrees, dumping a batch of food that blasts open the scatter cone.
  4. Saturday: The feeder is now hanging 4 feet lower, almost touching the water, empty and ready for a refill.

turns.prompt_text: How do I design the mechanical snail cam, trip lever, and escapement to snap the drum forward 45 degrees?
turns.response_html:
To achieve that sudden, violent 45-degree snap required to punch open your moisture-lock cone, you need to isolate the slow rotation of the governor spool from the food drum.

You can accomplish this using a Spring-Loaded Pawl and Star-Detent Mechanism. It consists of four distinct 3D-printed layers acting together: the timer, the hammer, the indexer, and the brake.

Here is the mechanical layout for designing this in OpenSCAD or your preferred CAD software.

Layer 1: The Snail Cam (The Timer)

Attached directly to your slow-moving governor spool is the snail cam.

  • Geometry: This is an Archimedean spiral. The radius gradually increases over a set angle (e.g., 355 degrees), ending in a sheer vertical drop-off back to the starting radius.
  • Function: If you want two feedings per spool rotation, you use a "double snail" (two 180-degree lobes).
  • The Follower: A pivoting lever arm rides against this cam. To prevent the plastic from wearing out under the heavy spring tension, design a post on the lever to hold a standard 608ZZ skate bearing to act as the cam roller.

Layer 2: The Trip Lever & Drive Pawl (The Hammer)

This is where the potential energy is stored and released.

  • The Arm: A rigid lever pivots on a fixed chassis pin. The cam slowly pushes this arm outward, stretching a heavy-duty steel extension spring (readily available at hardware stores).
  • The Drive Pawl: Mounted on the tip of the lever is a smaller, hinged finger (the pawl), pushed lightly inward by a small pen spring.
  • The Action: As the snail cam slowly lifts the arm, the pawl drags backward over the drum's ratchet gear, clicking softly over the teeth. When the cam follower reaches the cliff edge, the heavy spring violently slams the arm back to its starting position. The pawl catches a tooth and thrusts the drum forward.

Layer 3: The 8-Tooth Ratchet (The Indexer)

Attached directly to the bottom of the multi-tier food drum.

  • Geometry: A gear with 8 asymmetrical, saw-tooth shaped teeth (since you have 8 food pockets, $360° / 8 = 45°$).
  • The Catch: The flat face of the tooth must be angled slightly inward (an undercut of ~5 degrees) so that when the drive pawl slams into it, the pawl is pulled deeper into the root of the tooth rather than slipping off.

Layer 4: The Star Wheel Detent (The Brake & Aligner)

This is the most critical part of the design. A drum full of fish food is heavy. When you snap it forward, its angular momentum will cause it to spin right past 45 degrees, potentially dumping two or three days of food at once.

  • Geometry: Mounted above or below the ratchet is an 8-lobed wavy star wheel (imagine a gear with deep, smooth, U-shaped valleys and rounded peaks).
  • The Brake: A separate, heavily spring-loaded arm holds a second 608 bearing. This bearing sits firmly in one of the star wheel's valleys.
  • How it works: When the drive pawl slams the drum forward, it has enough force to push the star wheel so the bearing rides up over the peak. As soon as it crosses the peak, the bearing snaps down into the next valley, arresting the drum's momentum instantly and locking the next pocket perfectly over the drop port.

Assembly Stack Summary

[ Central Slow-Rotating Spool Shaft ] ──> Snail Cam (Layer 1)
                  │
[ Fixed Chassis / Non-Rotating Base ] ──> Pivot points for Lever & Detent
                  │
[ Free-Spinning Segmented Food Drum ] ──> Ratchet (Layer 3) & Star Wheel (Layer 4)

OpenSCAD Design Tips for the Bambu A1

Since you are printing on a Bambu A1, you have great dimensional accuracy (~0.15mm tolerance), which is perfect for these mechanisms.

  1. Cam Drop-Off Angle: Do not make the drop-off perfectly radial (90 degrees to the center). Give it a slight 3 to 5-degree slope. If it's a perfect 90-degree cliff, the roller bearing can catch or scrape on the way down.
  2. Spring Anchors: Don't just print plastic posts for the heavy extension spring—under continuous load, PETG will experience creep and bend over time. Instead, design captive hex slots to insert M3 or M4 bolts and hook the spring directly to the metal threads.
  3. Print Orientation: The Snail Cam, Ratchet, and Trip Lever must all be printed flat on the bed. If you print them vertically, the layer lines will shear off under the snapping force of the spring.

turns.prompt_text: How do I engineer the governor or viscous damper to control the spool's descent rate so it lasts an entire week?
turns.response_html:
To make a 4-foot drop last an entire week, the spool needs to rotate incredibly slowly—exactly one revolution per day.

While a viscous rotary damper seems like the simplest solution, it will fail in an outdoor environment. The silicone oil inside dampers is highly temperature-dependent; the feeder would drop rapidly during a hot summer afternoon and freeze completely overnight.

To get reliable, temperature-independent timing, you need a mechanical escapement. The most reliable way to build this without machining tiny brass clock parts is to harvest a mechanical timer from a discarded appliance or cheap device and couple it to a 3D-printed gear train.

Here is how to engineer the gravity drive and governor.

1. The Spool Math

If you want the feeder to drop ~4 feet (1200 mm) over exactly 7 days, the spool must rotate exactly 1 time per day.

  • Required Circumference: $1200\text{ mm} / 7\text{ rotations} \approx 171.4\text{ mm}$
  • Target Spool Diameter: $171.4\text{ mm} / \pi \approx 54.5\text{ mm}$ (approx. 2.15 inches)

If you print a 54.5 mm diameter spool, every 360-degree rotation drops the feeder by exactly one day's allowance, making it extremely easy to align a double-lobed snail cam (yielding two feedings per day).

2. Harvesting the Governor

Rather than printing a complex balance wheel and anchor escapement, harvest a heavy-duty mechanical wind-up timer (like a 12-hour mechanical irrigation timer or a 60-minute kitchen timer).

  1. Remove the Mainspring: Open the timer and remove the coiled metal mainspring. You do not need it because the gravity of the suspended feeder will act as the power source.
  2. The Escapement Core: What remains is a pre-built, highly accurate gear train connected to a tiny balance wheel (the part that rapidly ticks back and forth).
  3. The Input Shaft: The central shaft where the dial used to sit is now your governor's input shaft. If you apply rotational torque to this shaft, the escapement will allow it to turn at a strictly regulated speed.

3. The 3D-Printed Gear Train (The Multiplier)

If you harvest a standard 12-hour mechanical timer, its input shaft is geared to rotate once every 12 hours. But your spool needs to rotate once every 24 hours.

To bridge this gap, you design a simple spur gear set in OpenSCAD to sit between your spool and the timer.

  • The Ratio: You need a 1:2 gear ratio.
  • The Setup: Print a large 60-tooth gear and attach it to your 54.5 mm spool. Print a smaller 30-tooth pinion gear and mount it directly onto the harvested timer's input shaft.
  • The Result: The heavy feeder pulls down on the rope, trying to spin the spool. The spool's 60-tooth gear pushes against the timer's 30-tooth gear. The timer's internal escapement clicks away, physically preventing the 30-tooth gear from rotating any faster than 2 revolutions per day. Consequently, your spool is locked to exactly 1 revolution per day.

4. Managing the Load (Torque Isolation)

A full week's worth of fish food plus the printed drum will weigh several pounds. If you apply that full gravitational torque directly to the tiny gears inside a harvested kitchen timer, it will strip the plastic teeth instantly.

To protect the timer, use a Compound Block and Tackle for your suspension rope.

Instead of hanging the feeder directly from a single strand of rope, rig the rope through a small 3D-printed pulley block at the top cable, then down to the feeder's spool. A 4-part pulley system reduces the tension on the spool to 1/4th of the feeder's total weight. This drastically lowers the sheer torque placed on the gear train while still providing enough continuous force to run the mechanism and stretch the trip-spring.
